newsitem.title: UK: Britain's OFT stirs pensions debate.
newsitem.headline: Britain's OFT stirs pensions debate.

text.p: Millions of Britons are losing out because of shortcomings in pension provision, according to a hard-hitting report from the Office of Fair Trading (OFT) published on Tuesday.
Director General of Fair Trading John Bridgeman said radical changes were needed if consumer interests were to be adequately safeguarded.

He attacked the performance of fund managers, calling on government ministers in future pensions policy to incorporate a new passively managed product -- one which tracks market performance rather than trying to achieve better returns by active selection of investments.
Existing pension products, he said, were marketed in an unnecessarily complex way, emphasising superior investment performance which Bridgeman described as "insubstantial and illusory".
"There is no convincing evidence that fund managers can consistently outperform the market over the period of a pension plan although the industry does not like to face up to this," he said.
The OFT criticised personal pension plans for providing poor value with benefits frequently being eroded by the high cost of marketing and fund management.
While it said that occupational pensions might have improved in recent years, those who left early -- as the majority do -- lost out.

Today's report comes at a bad time for the beleaguered pensions industry, already reeling from heavy criticisms of its handling of the pensions misselling scandal of the late 1980s and early 1990s when as many as 1-1/2 million people may have been wrongly advised to opt out of occupational schemes.
Later this week the government is expected to launch its own wide-ranging review of pensions provision.
It welcomed the report and the OFT's proposal of a new pension product - the designated personal pension (DPP).

"The aims which lie behind the designated personal pension proposal reflect the government's belief that a new framework for value for money, flexible and secure second pensions should be developed," said pensions minister John Denham.
The response from the pensions industry was more circumspect.
A spokesman for Britain's largest life insurance group Prudential Corp said anything that advocated flexibility and extending coverage to everyone was to be welcomed.
But he rejected criticism of active fund management which he defended as producing superior investment performance and adding value to policies.
Legal & General said that experience showed that the majority of people still wanted face to face advice.
The OFT's proposed DPP would provide a portable, 'defined contribution' scheme and would need to be adequately funded, where appropriate, by the employer, Bridgeman said.
It would not penalise those who changed jobs nor have to bear heavy fund management and distribution costs.
Wide provision should be encouraged by changes to the tax system, he said but drew back from calling for it to be mandatory.
Alongside existing providers, the OFT envisaged alternative channels for the DPP, such as building societies or unions.

It would do away with the higher costs associated with active fund management and be designed to provide more flexible pension arrangements, encouraging those falling through the pensions net to take out provision.
Around 25 percent of the workforce have no pension provision and some 45 percent of the population will rely on the state for income unless adequate provision is made.

The OFT inquiry, launched in September 1996, attacked the way expenses of personal pension plans were often loaded onto the early years of the plan and weighed disproportionately on those discontinuing the pension.
Employees in occupational pension schemes who moved employers several times could find their occupational pension up to 30 percent lower than someone who stayed in the same scheme.
The pension rights that employees received on leaving 'defined benefit' schemes were also subject to a large degree of actuarial discretion which could dramatically reduce their size.
